name: Shabby Chic
reacts_against: both overly formal, untouchable "museum" antique display and sterile modern minimalism, favoring furniture that looks lived-in, loved and gently distressed instead.
article: Shabby chic has an unusually clean paper trail for an interior-design style: British designer Rachel Ashwell opened a Santa Monica shop under that exact name in 1989, built around deliberately distressed, white-painted antique furniture and faded floral linen, and codified the look nationally with her 1996 book Shabby Chic. The style's core idea — elegance that looks gently aged and used rather than pristine — positioned it against both overly formal antique collecting (where pieces are treated as untouchable museum objects) and the sterile, hard-edged minimalism dominant in 1990s interior design media. Ashwell's brand built a substantial retail business around the aesthetic through the 1990s-2000s, and the look's soft, faded palette and love of secondhand and inherited objects anticipated several later trends by decades, grandmillennial decorating in particular revives much of the same chintz-and-antique sensibility for a different generation.
